title: Strings, pointer arrays, and argv
summary: Handle text as bytes: character codes, strings that end in a zero byte, tables of string addresses, and the arguments main receives.

body.markdown:
Read these first:

- [External data: .data, .bss, and .text](/learn/external-data)
- [Subroutines: saved registers, pointers, and big arguments](/learn/calling-conventions)

To a program, text is nothing but bytes in memory. This lesson reads and changes text one byte at a time, builds a table of strings, and reads the words typed after a program's name on the command line.

## Characters are numbers

A computer stores text as numbers, one per character. The table that pairs each character with its number is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange): `'A'` is 65, `'a'` is 97, `'0'` is 48, a space is 32 and a newline is 10. Every code fits in one byte.

You never need to look the numbers up. A *character constant*, one character between single quotes, stands for its code, so `mov w10, 'a'` puts 97 in `w10` and `cmp w10, 'z'` compares with 122. Arithmetic works on them too: `'a' - 'A'` is 32, the distance from any capital letter to its lower-case partner.

The letters come in order, so `'a'` to `'z'` is one unbroken range, and so are `'A'` to `'Z'` and `'0'` to `'9'`. A digit character is not its value: `'7'` is 55, and subtracting `'0'` leaves 7.

## A string is bytes ending in zero

A *string* is a run of character codes in consecutive bytes, followed by one byte holding 0, called the *terminator* (or null byte). The label on a string is the address of its first byte. Nothing records the length, so any code that walks a string, `printf`'s `%s` included, reads bytes until it meets the 0.

Three directives put text in memory:

| Directive | What it stores |
|---|---|
| `.string "hi"` | 3 bytes: `'h'`, `'i'`, 0 |
| `.asciz "hi"` | the same 3 bytes; another spelling of `.string` |
| `.ascii "hi"` | 2 bytes: `'h'`, `'i'`, and no terminator |

Text made with `.ascii` has no end marker, so `%s` runs on into whatever follows it in memory. Use `.string` unless you are joining pieces by hand.

## Walking a string one byte at a time

`ldrb` loads one byte into a register and fills the rest of the register with zeros; `strb` stores the lowest byte of a register. Together they let a program read and change a string one character at a time.

The program below points `x9` at the first byte of a note. For each byte before the terminator, it checks whether the byte lies between `'a'` and `'z'`. If it does, subtracting 32 turns it into the matching capital, and `strb` writes it back in the same place. The note is in `.data`, so the program is allowed to change it. The loop loads each byte in its test, so an empty string, which is only a terminator, runs the body zero times. It prints:

body.source:
before: Meet me at 9, by the old oak.
after:  MEET ME AT 9, BY THE OLD OAK.

body.starter:
// Visit each byte of a string up to the zero byte, upper-casing letters

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(ptr_r, x9)
define(ch_r, w10)

.data
note_m:     .string "Meet me at 9, by the old oak."
fmt_before: .string "before: %s\n"
fmt_after:  .string "after:  %s\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        ldr     x0, =fmt_before
        ldr     x1, =note_m
        bl      printf

        ldr     ptr_r, =note_m
        b       walk_test
walk_loop:
        cmp     ch_r, 'a'
        b.lt    walk_next                   // below 'a': not a lower-case letter
        cmp     ch_r, 'z'
        b.gt    walk_next                   // above 'z': not one either
        sub     ch_r, ch_r, 'a' - 'A'       // 'a' - 'A' is 32, the gap between the cases
        strb    ch_r, [ptr_r]
walk_next:
        add     ptr_r, ptr_r, 1
walk_test:
        ldrb    ch_r, [ptr_r]
        cmp     ch_r, 0
        b.ne    walk_loop                   // the zero byte marks the end

        ldr     x0, =fmt_after
        ldr     x1, =note_m
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout:
before: Meet me at 9, by the old oak.
after:  MEET ME AT 9, BY THE OLD OAK.

## An array of pointers to strings

Strings differ in length, so they cannot sit in a table where every entry has the same size. Their addresses can, since every address is 8 bytes. `.dword` stores 8-byte values, and a label written as a value stands for its address, so this line builds a table of four addresses, 32 bytes in all:

```text
phrases_m:  .dword hello_m, bonjour_m, hola_m, salaam_m
```

Entry `i` starts at `phrases_m + i * 8`, so the index is scaled by 8: `ldr x2, [table_r, pick_r, SXTW 3]` (a left shift by 3 multiplies by 8). What comes back is an address, ready for `%s`, and one `ldrb` through it reads the first letter. `.balign 8` in front of the table puts each address on an 8-byte boundary.

With `PICK` set to 2 the program prints `phrase 2 is hola, first letter h`. Change the `define` to 0, 1 or 3 and run it again.

body.starter:
// An array of pointers to strings, one entry picked by index

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(pick_r, w9)
define(table_r, x10)

define(PICK, 2)

.data
hello_m:    .string "hello"
bonjour_m:  .string "bonjour"
hola_m:     .string "hola"
salaam_m:   .string "salaam"

        .balign 8
phrases_m:  .dword hello_m, bonjour_m, hola_m, salaam_m    // four addresses, 8 bytes each

fmt_phrase: .string "phrase %d is %s, first letter %c\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        mov     pick_r, PICK
        ldr     table_r, =phrases_m
        ldr     x2, [table_r, pick_r, SXTW 3]   // x2 = phrases[pick]: an address, so scale by 8
        ldrb    w3, [x2]                    // the first byte of that string

        ldr     x0, =fmt_phrase
        mov     w1, pick_r
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout: phrase 2 is hola, first letter h

## argc and argv

When a program starts, the operating system passes `main` two arguments:

`argc`, in `w0`, counts the words on the command line, the program's own name included. `argv`, in `x1`, is the address of an array of pointers, one per word, built just like `phrases_m`: `argv[0]` points at the program's name, `argv[1]` at the first argument, and so on. After the last one sits an entry holding 0.

Every argument is a string, even one that looks like a number: `42` arrives as the bytes `'4'`, `'2'`, 0. The library function `atoi` turns a string like that into an `int`.

The program below prints `argc`, then walks `argv` from the last entry down to `argv[1]`, printing each argument and its length. The length comes from `strlen`, a library function that counts the bytes before the terminator. The walk stops before `argv[0]`, whose text depends on how the program was started. `argc`, `argv`, the index and the current argument all have to survive calls to `printf` and `strlen`, so they live in `x19` to `x22`, which `main` saves first.

The lesson runs it with the arguments `red green blue`, so it prints:

body.source:
argc = 4
argv[3] = blue, length 4
argv[2] = green, length 5
argv[1] = red, length 3

body.starter:
// Print argc, then each argument and its length, last to first

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(argc_r, w19)
define(argv_r, x20)
define(idx_r, w21)
define(arg_r, x22)

.data
fmt_argc:   .string "argc = %d\n"
fmt_arg:    .string "argv[%d] = %s, length %ld\n"

.text
// main(w0 = argc, x1 = argv) keeps four values across calls in x19 to x22,
// so it saves the caller's copies first
save_s = 16
alloc = -(16 + 32) & -16
dealloc = -alloc

        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, alloc]!
        mov     fp, sp
        stp     x19, x20, [fp, save_s]
        stp     x21, x22, [fp, save_s + 16]

        mov     argc_r, w0                  // argc and argv arrive in w0 and x1,
        mov     argv_r, x1                  // which the first printf would overwrite

        ldr     x0, =fmt_argc
        mov     w1, argc_r
        bl      printf

        sub     idx_r, argc_r, 1            // start at the last argument
        b       back_test
back_loop:
        ldr     arg_r, [argv_r, idx_r, SXTW 3]  // one entry: the address of that argument's text
        mov     x0, arg_r
        bl      strlen                      // x0 = its length in bytes

        mov     x3, x0
        ldr     x0, =fmt_arg
        mov     w1, idx_r
        mov     x2, arg_r
        bl      printf
        sub     idx_r, idx_r, 1
back_test:
        cmp     idx_r, 1
        b.ge    back_loop                   // stop before argv[0], the program's own name

        ldp     x19, x20, [fp, save_s]
        ldp     x21, x22, [fp, save_s + 16]
        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], dealloc
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout:
argc = 4
argv[3] = blue, length 4
argv[2] = green, length 5
argv[1] = red, length 3

body.markdown: To try other words, open the program in the playground and change the args box there. With the box empty, `argc` is 1 and the loop body never runs.

## Check yourself

1. What does `.string "ok"` store, byte by byte?
2. `x9` holds `argv`. Which instruction loads `argv[2]`, the address of the second argument's text?
3. A program reads the character `'7'` out of a string and wants to add seven to a total. What must it do first?
4. A program is started as `./a.out one two`. What is `argc`?

Answers:

1. Three bytes: 111 (`'o'`), 107 (`'k'`) and the terminator 0.
2. `ldr x10, [x9, 16]`. Entry 2 starts 2 times 8, or 16, bytes into the array.
3. Subtract `'0'`. The byte holds 55, the code for `'7'`, and 55 - 48 is 7.
4. 3: the program's name and the two arguments.
